'''bowel†''' (bou′el), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''boweled'' or ''bowelled'', ppr. ''boweling'' or ''bowelling''. [< ME. ''bowelen''; cf. OF. ''boeler''; from the noun.] To take out the bowels of; eviscerate; penetrate the bowels of; disembowel.
{{smaller block|Drawn and hanged in his armour, taken down alive and ''bowelled''.
{{right|''Stow'', Edward II., an. 1326.}}}}

'''bowelless†''' (bou′el-les), ''a.'' [< ''bowel'' + ''-less''.] Without tenderness or pity; unfeeling.
{{smaller block|Miserable men commiserate not themselves; ''bowelless'' unto others, and merciless unto their own bowels.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., i. 7.}}}}

'''bowel-pryer†''' (bou′el-prī″ėr), ''n.'' One who practises divination by examining the intestines of animals. ''Holland.''

'''bowel-prying†''' (bou′el-prī″ing), ''n.'' Divination by examining the bowels of animals. ''Holland.''

'''bowenite''' (bō′en-īt), ''n.'' [After George T. ''Bowen'', who described it in 1822.] A variety of serpentine from Smithfield, Rhode Island, of light-green color and fine granular texture. It is remarkable for its hardness and its resemblance to jade.

'''bower<sup>1</sup>''' (bou′ėr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''bour'', ''boure'', etc.; < ME. ''bour'', < AS. ''būr'', a dwelling, house, room, chamber (= OS. ''būr'' = MLG. ''būr'', a house, cage, LG. ''buur'', a cage, = OHG.
readings.c1s2:
''būr'', a chamber, MHG. ''būr'', G. ''bauer'', a cage, = Icel. ''būr'', a chamber, larder, store-room, = Sw. ''bur'' = Dan. ''bur'', formerly ''buur''), < ''būan'' = Icel. ''būa'', etc., dwell. Cf. ''booth'', ''bottle''<sup>1</sup>, ''build'', etc., from the same root. Hence ult. ''boor'', ''bower''<sup>5</sup>, and ''neigh-bour'', ''neigh-bor''.] '''1.''' A dwelling or habitation; particularly, a cottage; an unpretentious residence; a rustic abode. [Now only poetical.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Courtesy oft-times in simple ''bowers''
Is found as great as in the stately towers.</poem>
{{right|''Sir J. Harington'', tr. of Ariosto, xiv. 62.}}}}
'''2†.''' An inner room; any room in a house except the hall or public room; hence, a bedchamber.
{{smaller block|In hast came rushing forth from inner ''bowre.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 5.}}}}
'''3.''' Especially, a lady’s private chamber; a boudoir. [Poetical.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The feast was over in Branksome tower,
And the Ladye had gone to her secret ''bower.''</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., i. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' A shelter made with boughs or twining plants; an arbor; a shady recess.
{{smaller block|<poem>I only begged a little woodbine ''bower''
Where I might sit and weep.</poem>
{{right|''W. Mason'', English Garden, 3.}}}}

'''bower'''<sup>1</sup>† (bou′ėr), ''v.'' [< ''bower''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To inclose in a bower, or as in a bower; embower; inclose.
{{smaller block|<poem>O nature! what hadst thou to do in hell,
When thou didst ''bower'' the spirit of a fiend
In mortal paradise of such sweet flesh?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 2.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take shelter; lodge.

'''bower'''<sup>1</sup>† (bou′ėr), ''v.''   [< ''bower''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To inclose in a bower, or as in a bower; embower; inclose.
{{smaller block|<poem>O nature! what hadst thou to do in hell,
When thou didst ''bower'' the spirit of a fiend
In mortal paradise of such sweet flesh?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 2.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take shelter; lodge. {{smaller block|Spredding pavilions for the birds to ''bowre.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. x. 6.}}}}

'''bower'''<sup>2</sup> (bou′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bow''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who or that which bows or bends; specifically, a muscle that bends the joints.
{{smaller block|His rawbone armes, whose mighty brawned ''bowrs''
Were wont to rive steele plates.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 41.}}}}

'''bower'''<sup>3</sup> (bou′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bow''<sup>3</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   An anchor carried at the bow of a ship. {{smaller|The two bower-anchors were formerly of unequal size, and were called the ''best'' and ''small'' bower respectively; but when (as generally now) of equal size, they are known as the ''starboard'' and ''port'' bowers.}}
{{smaller block|The whaler . . . made a clumsy piece of work in getting her anchor, being obliged to let go her ''best bower'', and, finally, to get out a kedge and a hawser.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 250.}}}}

'''bower'''<sup>4</sup> (bou′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bow''<sup>3</sup>, 1, = ''bough''<sup>1</sup>, + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   In ''falconry'', a young hawk when it begins to leave the nest and to clamber on the boughs. Also called ''bowess'', ''bowet.''

'''bower'''<sup>5</sup>†, ''n.''   [Late ME. ''boueer'', < D. ''bouwer'', a farmer, peasant (in this sense prop. ''boer''), also a builder, = G. ''bauer'', a peasant, also a builder: see ''boor'', and cf. ''bower''<sup>6</sup>.]   A peasant; a farmer.

'''bower'''<sup>6</sup> (bou′ėr), ''n.''   [E. spelling of G. ''bauer'', a peasant, a farmer; in a German pack of cards, the knave or jack; = D. ''boer'', a farmer, the knave in cards, > E. ''boor'', q. v.]   In ''euchre'', one of the two highest cards, or, if the joker is used, the second or third highest. {{smaller|The bowers are the knave of trumps, the higher of the two, called the ''right bower'', and the knave of the suit having the same color as the trump, called the ''left bower''.}}
<poem>
But the hands that were played
By that heathen Chinee,
And the points that he made,
Were quite frightful to see —
Till at last he put down a ''right bower'',
Which the same Nye had dealt unto me.
</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Bret Harte'', Heathen Chinee.}}}}

'''bower'''<sup>7</sup> (bō′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bow''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' and ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''bowyer''.]   '''1†.''' A bow-maker; a bowyer.—'''2.''' One who plays with a bow on a violin or other stringed instrument.

'''bower'''<sup>8</sup> (bö′ėr or bou′ėr), ''n.''   [Also written ''booer''; < ''bow''<sup>5</sup>, a head of cattle, farm-stock, + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   A person who rents or leases the dairy stock on a farm, together with pasture and fodder for them, and makes what he can from their produce, the cultivation of the farm still remaining with the farmer or proprietor. [S. W. counties of Scotland.]

'''bower-anchor''' (bou′ėr-ang″ko̤r), ''n.'' An anchor carried at a ship’s bows. See ''bower''<sup>3</sup>.

'''bower-bird''' (bou′ėr-bėrd), ''n.'' The name of the Australian oscine passerine birds of the genera ''Ptilonorhynchus'', ''Chlamydodera'', etc., constituting with some authors a subfamily ''Ptilonorhynchinæ'', of the family ''Oriolidæ''. {{smaller|They are remarkable for building what are called bowers, runs, or playhouses, which they adorn with gay feathers, rags, bones, shells, and other white, bright, or conspicuous objects. There are several species of both the genera named; the best-known are the satin bower-bird, ''P. holosericeus'', and the spotted bower-bird, ''C. maculata''. The bowers are not the nests of the birds, but places of resort where they amuse themselves.}}

[[File:century v01 p0672 c2f1.png|center|264px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Satin Bower-bird (''Ptilonorhynchus holosericeus'').}}}}

'''bower-eaves''' (bou′ėr-ēvz), ''n. pl.'' The eaves of a bower or bedchamber.
{{smaller block|A bow-shot from her ''bower-eaves.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lady of Shalott, iii.}}}}

'''bowered''' (bou′ėrd), ''a.''   [< ''bower''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Furnished with bowers, recesses, or alcoves.   ''Tennyson.''

'''bowerly''' (bou′ėr-li), ''a.''   [See ''burly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Large; stout; burly. [Prov. Eng.]

'''bower-maid''' (bou′ėr-mād), ''n.''   [< ''bower''<sup>1</sup> + ''maid.'' Cf. ME. ''bourmaiden.'']   A young woman in attendance on a lady; a lady’s-maid; a waiting-woman. [Now only poetical.]

'''bower-thane''' (bou′ėr-thān), ''n.''   [Mod. form of ME. ''burthein'', < AS. ''būr-thegn'', < ''būr'', bower, + ''thegn'', thane.]   A chamberlain under the Saxon kings.
{{smaller block|The chamberlain, or ''bower-thane'', was also the royal treasurer. {{right|''Thorpe'', tr. of Lappenberg’s Hist. Eng., v.}}}}

'''bower-woman''' (bou′ėr-wu̇m″a̤n), ''n.'' Same as ''bower-maid. Scott.''

'''bowery'''<sup>1</sup> (bou′ėr-i), ''a.''   [< ''bower''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Of the nature of a bower; containing bowers; leafy; shady.

'''bowery'''<sup>2</sup> (bou′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''boweries'' (-iz).   [Also written ''bowerie'' and ''bouwery''; < D. ''bouwerij'', a farm, prop. farming, husbandry, < ''bouwer'', a farmer: see ''bower''<sup>5</sup> and ''boor.'']   Among the Dutch settlers of New York, a farm; a country-seat; a rural retreat. {{smaller|Hence the name of the ''Bowery'', a long, wide street in the city of New York, originally a road through the bowery or farm of Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch colonial governor of New Netherlands.}}
{{smaller block|A goodly ''bowerie'' or farm was allotted to the sage Oloffe in consideration of the service he had rendered to the public by his talent at dreaming.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 133.}}}}

'''bowess, bowet<sup>1</sup>''' (bou′es, -et), ''n.''   [See ''bower''<sup>4</sup>.]   In ''falconry'', a young hawk when it begins to leave the nest.

'''bowet<sup>1</sup>''' (bou′et), ''n.'' See ''bowess''.

'''bowet<sup>2</sup>''' (bö′et), ''n.'' Same as ''buat''.

'''bow-fast''' (bou′fȧst), ''n.''   ''Naut.'', a rope or chain by which a ship is secured at the bow.

'''bow-file''' (bō′fīl), ''n.'' A file having a bowed or curved edge; a riffler.

'''bowfin''' (bou′fin), ''n.'' A name of the mudfish, ''Amia calva.'' Also called ''brindle, grindle, lawyer, dogfish'', etc. See cut under ''Amiidæ.''

'''bowge†''', ''v.'' See ''bouge''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bow-grace''' (bou′grās), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a frame, or composition of junk, laid out at the sides, stem, or bows of a ship to secure it from injury by ice.

'''bow-hand''' (bō′hand), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''archery'', the hand that holds the bow, commonly the left hand.—'''2.''' In ''music'', the hand that draws the bow; a violinist’s right hand.—'''On the bow-hand.'''
{{smaller block|(''a'') On the wrong side; wrongly; inaccurately.}}
{{smaller block|He shootes wyde ''on the bowe hand'', and very farre from the marke.
{{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''b'') Wrong in one’s calculations.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Uber.'' Well, you must have this wench, then?
''Ric.'' I hope so;
I am much o’ ''the bow-hand'' else.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, i. 3.}}}}

'''bow-harpsichord''' (bō′härp″si-kôrd), ''n.'' Same as ''bow-clavier.''

'''bow-head''' (bō′hed), ''n.'' A species of right whale; the polar right whale or Greenland whale, ''Balæna mysticetus.'' See also cut under ''whale.''

'''bow-headed''' (bō′hed-ed), ''a.'' Having a bowed or bent head, as a right whale.

'''bowie''' (bou′i), ''n.''   [Perhaps from OF. ''buie'', prob. same as ''buire'', a water-pitcher, vessel for wine, < ''buire'', F. ''boire'', < L. ''bibere'', drink.]   A large wooden milk-bowl. [Scotch.]

'''bowie-knife''' (bō′ẹ̄-nīf; in the Southwest pronounced bö′ẹ̄-nīf), ''n.''   [After its inventor, Colonel James ''Bowie'', died 1836.]   A heavy sheath-knife first used in the early part of the present century in Kentucky and other parts of the United States which were then on the borders of civilization. {{smaller|The blade is from 9 to 10 inches long, and has only one edge; the back is straight for three}}
{{smaller|quarters of its length, and then curves toward the edge in a slightly concave sweep, while the edge finishes toward the point in a convex curve. The guard is very small, and the tongue is of the full breadth of the grip or barrel, which is formed of two rounded pieces of wood or bone. The best knives were made by frontier blacksmiths, of old horse-rasps and the like, and naturally differed much in size and pattern. The term is used at present for almost any large sheath-knife.}}

[[File:century v01 p0672 c3f1.png|center|275px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Bowie-knife and Sheath.}}}}

'''bowing<sup>1</sup>''' (bō′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''bow''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' The operation of separating and arranging as desired the filaments of some fibrous material, as hatters’ fur or (in Eastern countries) cotton, by vibrating a bow-string upon it. {{smaller|In hat-making, as practised on a small scale, the felting of the fur or wool is partly accomplished by bowing.}}

'''2.''' In ''music'': (''a'') The general method of using the bow in playing upon an instrument of the violin family. {{smaller|It includes the method of holding the bow, the direction in which it is moved, the pressure put upon it, the part of the hair that is employed, the place upon the strings where it is applied, and every other detail in the management of the bow which influences the quality and loudness of the tone produced.}} (''b'') The method by which the notes of a given passage are distributed between up- and down-strokes of the bow. {{smaller|To secure an intended effect, or general uniformity among many players, the ''bowing'' of a passage is indicated by various marks; ⊓ or ⊔ indicates a stroke beginning with the nut, that is, down; while ∨ or ∧ indicates a stroke beginning with the point, that is, up.}}

'''bowing'''<sup>2</sup> (bō′ing), ''n.''   [< ''bow''<sup>5</sup>, ''n.'', + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.]   A lease of the dairy stock on a farm. See ''bower''<sup>8</sup>. [Scotch.]

'''bowingly''' (bou′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a bending manner.   ''Huloet.''

'''bow-instrument''' (bō′in″strö-ment), ''n.'' A stringed instrument played by means of a bow, as the double-bass, the small bass or violoncello, the tenor, the violin proper, etc.

'''bow-iron''' (bō′ī″ėrn), ''n.'' A clasp or holder used to secure the bows of a carriage-top.

'''bowk'''<sup>1</sup> (bouk), ''n.'' Same as ''bulk''<sup>1</sup>.   [Scotch.]

'''bowk'''<sup>2</sup> (bouk), ''v. t.'' Same as ''buck''<sup>3</sup>.   [Scotch.]

'''bow-kail''' (bou′kāl), ''n.''   [Cf. ''borecole.'']   Cabbage.   ''Burns.'' [Scotch.]

'''bowking''' (bou′king), ''n.'' Same as ''bucking''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bow-knot''' (bō′not), ''n.'' A slip-knot made by drawing a portion of a cord, ribbon, etc., in the form of a bow through an involution, which is<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
